schools.summary: Matthew Henry makes 'the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus' a text on providence: the hearts of kings are in God's hand; a heathen monarch acts in pursuance of Jeremiah's word, honouring the prophet long after his death.

Clarke supplies Cyrus's parentage and Josephus's account that he was shown the Isaiah oracles naming him, likely by Daniel; Wesley works the seventy-years arithmetic and fixes 'first year' as first over Babylon.
Gill dates 'the first year of Cyrus' to his reign over Babylon, not Persia, weighing Cicero, Herodotus, and Africanus's Olympiad reckoning.
Keil and Delitzsch frame the book from its title, deriving its name from Ezra the priest and scribe.
Keil and Delitzsch match the proclamation to the Persian royal edicts of the cuneiform inscriptions, which credit Ahuramazd, noting Cyrus substitutes Jahve the God of heaven for Ormuzd.
Clarke marks 'God of heaven' as a post-exilic title and maps the vast Medo-Persian empire; Wesley credits the gift to God, moved by Isaiah's prophecy or a special illumination.
Henry reads the preamble as a double confession of gratitude and obedience, God being the fountain of power; the heathen king's obedience aggravates Israel's revolt.
Gill notes Isaiah prophesied of Cyrus and this edict two hundred years before his birth.

themes: all the kingdoms of the earth

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take 'all his people' of the whole nation of Israel, not Judah only; 'his God be with him' is a blessing (cf. Joshua 1:17), varying from 'the LORD his God' at 2 Chron. 36:23.
Gill extends the invitation to the ten tribes as well as Judah and Benjamin, since the edict ran through all Cyrus's dominions.
Henry marvels that Cyrus overlooked his own state interest ('piety is the best policy') and ordered a temple to the God of Israel, not to the gods of Babylon or Persia.

themes: the one true God in Jerusalem

schools.summary: Clarke reads the clause as liberty and trial: none was obliged to go, so the heart was tested; those who stayed were commanded to assist those who went.
Keil and Delitzsch set the provision within the edict: Cyrus requires all subjects to help the returning exiles and bring free-will offerings for the temple.
Gill identifies the beneficiary as the Israelite left behind through poverty, unable to bear the charges of the journey.
Henry reads a royal brief for a collection, weighing whether the aid is from the king's revenue (cf. Ezra 6:8) or the neighbours' alms; well-wishers to the temple should be well-doers for it.

themes: liberty and trial of the heart

schools.summary: Henry makes divinely-raised willingness the theme: leaders and ministers lead in duty; the return is 'not by might, nor by power' (Zech. 4:6); those who broke through the discouragements were those whose spirits God raised.
Keil and Delitzsch press the grammar: all were called, but only those God made willing obeyed; Josephus records that many stayed in Babylon rather than leave their possessions.
Gill names the leaders as princes of Judah and Benjamin and heads of families, with some of other tribes.
Wesley echoes Henry: this new generation went out like Abraham from the land of the Chaldees, not knowing whither (Heb. 11:8).

themes: the temptation to stay in Babylon

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch widen 'those about them' to heathen neighbours and Jews who stayed; 'strengthened their hands' means to give active aid (cf. Lev. 25:34), and the free-will gifts are for the house of God (cf. 1 Chron. 29:9).
Wesley marvels that God inclines strangers to strengthen the hands that once weakened Israel; Clarke glosses the 'vessels of silver' as articles of silver and gold.
Henry sees the pattern of the tabernacle's Egyptian spoils repeated, the second temple rising by Chaldean gifts, intimating the Gentiles' future admission; 'the earth helped the woman' (Rev. 12:16).
Gill identifies the givers plainly as the neighbours, the Chaldeans.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the vessels as those Nebuchadnezzar took at the first conquest and lodged in his god's treasure-house (2 Chron. 36:7; Dan. 1:2), explaining why the later-seized and broken vessels (2 Kings 24:13; 25:14; Jer. 52:18) were not among them.
Henry draws a double providence: God kept the vessels whole across seventy years (cf. 2 Tim. 2:19), and gave back for holy use what idols had profaned.
Gill notes Cyrus ordered the vessels brought forth.
Clarke reserves his fuller comment for the inventory, pointing ahead to the numbering of the vessels.
Keil and Delitzsch identify Sheshbazzar as Zerubbabel under his Chaldee name, grounding the identity in Ezra 5:14 and the leadership Ezra 2:2 and 3:8 assign to Zerubbabel.
Clarke and Wesley read the two names ('joy in affliction' / 'a stranger in Babylon'); Clarke alone records the view that Sheshbazzar was a separate Persian or Chaldean commissioner.
Gill glosses Mithredath the treasurer, a Persian name from the sun-god Mithras.
Henry dwells on Judah having a prince of David's house even in captivity, to whom the vessels were numbered out for safe conveyance.

debates.question: Is Sheshbazzar the same man as Zerubbabel?

sides.position: Sheshbazzar is Zerubbabel under his Chaldee name
Sheshbazzar was a separate Persian or Chaldean officer sent by Cyrus to superintend the return

themes: a prince of Judah in captivity

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch labour over two words found only here: 'chargers' (a basin or basket, not the blood-vessels the rabbis imagined) and 'knives' (a term for piercing/cutting, cf. Judg. 5:26; Job 20:24), weighing each rendering with hesitation.
Gill presents the numbered list as the faithful discharge of the sacred trust, each class of vessel counted out to the prince of Judah.
Gill reads the gold 'basons' either as covered cups or, with Jarchi and Aben Ezra, as the vessels that received and sprinkled the blood of the sacrifices at the altar.

Keil and Delitzsch begin totalling the figures toward the grand sum, noting the enumerated 2,499 (as in the Septuagint) and rejecting as arbitrary the reconciliation that only the larger vessels were listed (cf. 2 Chron. 36:18).

Gill reconciles the totals: the enumerated 2,499 are the larger vessels, the sum 5,400 takes in great and small, and the fuller letter of Cyrus itemizes them to exactly 5,400 (apocryphal Esdras, 5,469).

Clarke judges the place manifestly corrupt, correcting from the apocryphal Esdras (5,469, only 69 different), and rules out the 'chief only specified' escape on the ground of the 'other vessels a thousand.'
Keil and Delitzsch hold the verse is indisputably a sum-total of the separate numbers, so the older harmonizing is arbitrary.
Henry marks Sheshbazzar's safe conveyance of the vessels home, and reads the lasting comfort that God's ordinances, though profaned by a later Babylon, shall be restored to their primitive use.

debates.question: How is the total of 5,400 to be reconciled with the enumerated 2,499?

sides.position: the figures can be squared: the list gives only the larger vessels, the total great and small together
the text is corrupt; a copyist's error has entered the numbers
